questions.learningObjective: Identify what a technology standard actually constrains
questions.stem: Memo 12/3: the district's appliance standard now requires new units below a set efficiency level, and suppliers must report the share of models meeting it. What does that standard actually deliver?

options.text: A minimum efficiency for each new unit sold, so performance rises without touching units already in use.
A guaranteed reduction in the stock's average efficiency each year.
options.misconception: assumes a standard retrofits the existing stock of appliances

options.text: A cap on the number of new appliances sold each year.
options.misconception: confuses an efficiency standard with a sales quota

options.text: A guaranteed average efficiency across every appliance in use.
options.misconception: believes new standards cover appliances already installed

questions.explanation: A standard sets a floor on the efficiency of new products, so it changes what is sold, not what is installed. The stock improves as it turns over, but no guaranteed yearly gain follows from the rule itself.
questions.hint: Ask whether old units are affected at all.

questions.stem: What was the total support paid out under the scheme last year?

options.misconception: adds the cap to the payment instead of limiting it

options.text: 22,080, from 3,000 kWh at 0.08 each across the 92 approved installations.
Zero, because the modelled use is an estimate rather than a metered figure.
options.misconception: refuses to pay out because the savings are modelled

options.text: 55,200, from 3,000 kWh multiplied by 0.08 and then by 600 installations.
options.misconception: confuses the cap with the number of installations

questions.explanation: Each installation attracts 3,000 times 0.08, which is 240, below the 600 cap, and 92 installations give 92 times 240, or 22,080. The cap limits a single large claim; it does not set everyone's payment.
questions.hint: Work out the payment per installation before multiplying.

options.text: The phase-out cut the number of CFC units by 80 per cent, though a small stock remains.
The remaining 120 units now hold all the market share in the district.
options.misconception: assumes the remaining units dominate a changed market

options.text: CFC units still account for 120 of the 600 cooling systems still running.
options.misconception: reads the remaining count as part of the original fleet total

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Plan an independent check of a self-declared emissions target
questions.stem: Memo: the district wants to check whether a country's self-declared target is being met without trusting the country's own reporting. Describe the assessment you would carry out.

answer.exemplar: I would rebuild the target's inventory from sector data I can inspect: plant-level fuel use, electricity import and export figures, and vehicle registrations, then compare the total against the target year using the same accounting boundaries the declaration used, since a change of boundary alone can create apparent progress. I would check the declared baseline, because a target measured against a generous base year is easier to hit, and record the gap in physical units as well as in index form. Any difference from the official figure would be reported with the sector that explains it rather than as a single verdict.

questions.explanation: A self-declared target is only checkable if the inventory, baseline year and boundaries can be reproduced. Rebuilding the total independently and reconciling sector by sector shows whether the declared progress is real.
questions.hint: Rebuild the total and check the baseline year.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain leakage and the scope of a border adjustment
questions.stem: Memo: a district introduces a carbon price and a neighbouring country does not. Explain what leakage means here and what a border adjustment is meant to do about it.

answer.exemplar: Leakage occurs when the carbon price pushes production, jobs or demand to the jurisdiction that has no price, so the world's total emissions may barely fall while the local number looks good. A border adjustment levels the field by requiring importers to pay the difference between the domestic carbon price and the price in the exporting country, or to hand in foreign allowances for the embedded carbon. It can reduce the incentive to relocate production, though it only works for traded goods, needs an accurate estimate of embedded emissions, and can raise costs for exporters that have never paid a carbon price.

questions.explanation: Leakage shifts production or demand to places without a carbon price, weakening the local gain. A border adjustment targets traded goods by charging importers the difference, but it does little for services that cannot be relocated.
questions.hint: Ask which production can move and which cannot.

options.text: The regulator sets the allowance price directly in line with the falling cap.
options.misconception: believes the regulator fixes the allowance price

options.text: Each firm sets its own price for emissions, so the market average emerges by itself.
options.misconception: assumes firms set the allowance price themselves

options.text: The price is the same as the tax rate in neighbouring districts.
options.misconception: links the allowance price to another scheme's tax rate

options.text: Trading between firms sets the price, and scarcity of allowances makes it rise as the cap tightens.

questions.explanation: A cap fixes quantity and lets trading set the price: a tighter cap makes allowances scarcer, so their price rises until firms cut enough emissions. The regulator sets the cap, not the price.
questions.hint: A cap fixes quantity; the market sets price.

questions.learningObjective: Identify free-riding in a voluntary scheme and its effect on measured savings

stimulus.body: The district's voluntary building scheme lets owners sign up for an efficiency standard in return for marketing support and a lower certificate fee. Sixty buildings have joined, and the administrator notes that many other owners in the same streets have not signed up but have begun buying certified units from the same suppliers.

questions.stem: What does the brief suggest about free-riding in the scheme?

options.text: Unjoined owners buy the same certified units, so measured savings understate the scheme's real influence.
Free-riding is impossible, because joining is the only way to reach certified suppliers.
options.misconception: assumes certified suppliers can serve only members

options.text: The 60 joined buildings show that voluntary schemes always crowd out regulation.
options.misconception: reads one scheme's uptake as proof about all voluntary schemes

options.text: Free-riding applies only to households, since commercial owners join by choice.
options.misconception: restricts free-riding to households rather than firms

questions.explanation: Free-riding means non-participants gain from the scheme's effects without contributing, here by buying the certified equipment it made available. That gain is missing from the scheme's own savings figure, so the number understates its influence.
questions.hint: Ask who benefits without joining or paying.

options.misconception: assumes a tax is always more cost-effective than a cap

options.text: The cap is the stronger instrument, because its lower price means it cuts more.
options.misconception: assumes a lower carbon price delivers deeper cuts

The prices are not comparable, because a tax and a cap are different currencies.
options.misconception: treats prices per tonne as incomparable between schemes

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Compare verifiability of payments per unit saved and per unit installed
questions.stem: Memo: the district pays households 0.12 per kilowatt-hour for electricity saved, verified from a baseline year. Explain why paying per unit saved can be harder to check than paying per unit of new equipment installed.

answer.exemplar: A payment per unit saved requires a counterfactual: the household's baseline use has to be estimated and adjusted for weather, occupancy and any other change, and if that baseline was set generously the payment over-rewards the household. Paying per item installed checks a visible fact instead, such as the cost of a heat pump, though it rewards installation rather than performance and does nothing about the units that never get replaced. Neither measure is a guarantee of a tonne of carbon saved.

questions.explanation: Payments per unit saved depend on an estimated baseline, so they inherit its error and can over-reward. Payments per item installed are easier to verify but reward purchase rather than performance.
questions.hint: One measure needs a counterfactual baseline.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify weaknesses in a self-declared percentage emissions target
questions.stem: Memo: a country declares a 40 per cent cut in emissions by 2035 against 2010. Explain two weaknesses that a planner should keep in mind when judging such a declaration.

answer.exemplar: The first weakness is the baseline: a target measured against 2010 can look easy if 2010 was an unusually high or low year, and a country with rising output may meet the percentage while its absolute emissions keep rising. The second is the reliance on self-declaration: without independent checks on the inventory, the accounting boundaries and the treatment of removals, the reported progress cannot be verified and the promise carries little pressure. A target also says nothing about who bears the cost.

questions.explanation: A percentage target hides its baseline, and a chosen base year can flatter the arithmetic. Self-declaration without independent inventory checks adds verifiability risk on top of the accounting choices.
questions.hint: Check the base year and who verifies the figures.

questions.learningObjective: Rank policy options by cost per tonne abated

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A flat cap against a growing sector
questions.learningObjective: Plan a review of a flat cap in a fast-growing sector
questions.stem: Memo: the district's industrial cap has been flat since 1990 while output tripled. Design the review you would run to set the next cap.

answer.exemplar: I would rebuild the sector's inventory by subsector so that growth is visible where it is happening, and separate output growth from structural change, since a shift towards lighter manufacturing can raise output without raising energy use. I would then examine the abatement options available at the current price of emissions, including efficiency, fuel switching and process change, and ask where the cost curve is now rather than where it was when the cap was set. The review should state the cap as an absolute limit and publish the intensity path that would be needed for output growth to stay inside it.

questions.explanation: A flat cap in a growing sector must be reviewed against today's technology and structure, not the ones in place when it was set. Rebuilding the inventory by subsector shows where growth and abatement options sit before a new number is chosen.
questions.hint: Rebuild the inventory and the abatement options first.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Compare the design of a carbon tax and a cap on trade
questions.stem: Memo: the council is choosing between a carbon tax and a cap and trade for the district's transport. Explain how the two differ in what they control and in what they leave uncertain.

answer.exemplar: A carbon tax fixes the price of carbon and leaves the quantity of emissions to the firms and households that respond, so emissions fall by however much is needed to reach the price, with the regulator never needing to know that number in advance. A cap fixes the quantity and lets trading set the price, so the regulator controls the outcome but must accept a price it does not set and adjust the cap if the price proves far too high or too low to shift investment. Where the regulator's information about abatement costs is weak, that difference decides which instrument is safer.

questions.explanation: A tax fixes price and lets quantity respond; a cap fixes quantity and lets price respond. A tax needs no knowledge of abatement costs, while a cap leaves the price and the investment signal uncertain.
questions.hint: One fixes price, the other fixes quantity.

questions.learningObjective: Design an evaluation that justifies extending a voluntary scheme
questions.stem: Memo: the council wants to extend the voluntary building scheme to firms that never joined, because those firms appear to be benefiting already. Describe the evaluation and the decision rule you would use.

answer.exemplar: I would first measure how much of the scheme's measured effect actually reaches non-participants, by comparing the equipment purchases of joined and unjoined firms in the same streets and asking whether the unjoined firms would have bought certified units anyway. I would then set the extension decision on additional tonnes rather than on firm numbers, so the council pays only for reductions that would not have happened without the support. I would record the cost of that extension against the cost per additional tonne, publish the free-riding estimate alongside the headline savings, and state plainly how much of the benefit the scheme would still be credited with.

questions.explanation: Free-riding means part of the benefit arrives without the scheme's money, so an extension must be judged on additional tonnes, not on the number of sites signed up. Measuring the reach among non-participants is what sets that number.

options.misconception: treats a smaller forecast cut as evidence of a better outcome

options.text: The tax, because it delivers a bigger cut and reuses the revenue for transport.
Neither, because the two options use different forecasts and cannot be compared.
options.misconception: declares two comparable options incomparable without cause

options.text: The tax, but only because its revenue makes the forecast cut easier to achieve.
options.misconception: credits revenue recycling with causing the emissions cut

questions.explanation: On the paper's numbers the tax delivers a larger cut and recycles revenue into transport. The cap's advantage would be certainty about the emissions quantity, which the paper's forecast does not address.

The scheme had no effect, because recycling volumes always rise over time.
options.misconception: dismisses the timing of the change as coincidental

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a small stock of ozone-depleting equipment persists
questions.stem: Memo: the district's refrigeration fleet still has CFC chillers. Explain why the remaining stock can persist so long after the phase-out began.

answer.exemplar: The leftover units are usually the ones where replacement is hardest: small shops with tight premises, high costs of downtime and equipment bought second-hand, so the capital cost and disruption exceed what they can afford. Their owners also capture less of the benefit, because the escaping refrigerant is a fraction of the shop's costs. Where the servicing trade still holds CFC, the remaining stock keeps being refilled rather than scrapped, so the programme has to run to the end of the equipment's life, not just the end of the sales ban.

questions.explanation: The remaining units are typically small, capital-poor sites where replacement costs and disruption outweigh the direct benefit of avoiding the refrigerant. Servicing can also keep the substance in circulation long after sales stopped.
questions.hint: Think about who cannot afford to replace equipment.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: How a cap sets a price
questions.learningObjective: Explain the shadow price meaning of an allowance price
questions.stem: Memo: explain to the council why the allowance price under a cap is described as the shadow price of carbon, and what it must not be confused with.

answer.exemplar: The allowance price is what it costs firms to buy the right to emit one more tonne, so it shows how much emitting is valued at the margin inside the cap: if the price is 30, the last tonne of the cap is worth 30 to the firms bidding for it. It is not a tax set by the regulator, because the regulator fixes the cap and the market fixes the price, and it is not necessarily the same as a carbon tax rate in another scheme, since two jurisdictions can hold different caps and still have the same allowance price. It is also not a forecast of the damage a tonne causes.

questions.explanation: The allowance price reveals what a tonne is worth to firms constrained by the cap, which is why it acts as a shadow price. It is set by trading, not by the regulator, and need not match another scheme's tax rate.
questions.hint: It is what the market pays for the right to emit.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a like-for-like comparison of two policy instruments
questions.stem: Memo: the council must choose between a grant scheme and a carbon price for district heating. Describe the comparison you would put in the paper.

answer.exemplar: I would compare the two on the same footing: tonnes of emissions avoided in a stated year, the public cost of each option including administration, and how the cost is distributed. For the grant I would use the administrative cost per tonne from actual take-up rather than the headline grant rate, and for the price I would model abatement responses at several price levels to find the cost of a given tonne of reduction, then compare that with the grant's cost for the same tonne. I would also record which reductions would have happened anyway, and note how each option affects household bills, since that determines whether it survives politically.

questions.explanation: Cost-effectiveness only means something when both options are measured the same way: the same tonnes, the same year, the same accounting of administrative cost, and the same treatment of reductions that would have happened anyway.
questions.hint: Compare the same tonne of reduction on both sides.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a standard can outperform a grant scheme in coverage
questions.stem: Memo: the district's appliance standard requires a minimum efficiency for new units. Explain why this can be more effective than a scheme that pays owners to upgrade.

answer.exemplar: A standard changes the default product, so every buyer of a new unit gets a better one without anyone applying for support or spending their own attention and money. It reaches all new sales rather than the subset willing to complete an application, and the benefit arrives as a lower price or a better model rather than a cheque. It is blunt where technologies differ, so it can exclude the cheapest options and raise costs for some households, but for a widely sold product it usually beats a voluntary programme at the same public cost.

questions.explanation: A standard reaches every new sale, including buyers who would never claim support, and the improvement arrives with the product rather than through an application. Its weakness is bluntness: one threshold can exclude cheap models.
questions.hint: It reaches buyers who never apply for anything.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which instrument gives certainty about quantity
questions.stem: Memo: the council wants a policy whose effect on the quantity of emissions it can predict with confidence. Which instrument fits that description best, and why?

options.text: A carbon tax, because the regulator can set the tax to hit a target quantity.
options.misconception: believes a tax fixes the emissions quantity

options.text: A cap, because the quantity of emissions is fixed by the regulator in advance.
Either, because the two instruments are equivalent in their effect on quantity.
options.misconception: treats a tax and a cap as interchangeable on quantity

options.text: Neither, because no instrument can fix emissions in advance with certainty.
options.misconception: denies that any instrument fixes a quantity

questions.explanation: A cap states the permitted quantity directly, so that outcome is known before trading begins, though the price is not. A tax fixes the price instead and leaves the quantity to be discovered.
questions.hint: One instrument fixes the amount allowed.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a trial comparing a per-unit payment with a fixed grant
questions.stem: Memo: the council must choose between paying households per kilowatt-hour saved and giving a fixed grant towards new equipment. Describe the trial you would run to compare the two.

answer.exemplar: I would recruit comparable households and meter them all for a full year, then apply the per-unit payment to one group and the grant to a second group with a third group waiting a year as a control. I would measure the same things in both: metered consumption, the capital cost each household had to find, and the hours of disruption from installation, since a grant that leaves households unable to finance the rest of a boiler achieves little. I would then compare the change in consumption and the cost per tonne abated on both sides, and check whether households who could not afford the matching grant dropped out, because that distributional effect matters as much as the average.

questions.explanation: A per-unit payment and a grant act on different margins, so the trial must measure consumption, capital cost and dropout on both sides. Cost per tonne alone would hide who the schemes reach.
questions.hint: Measure consumption, capital cost and dropout on both sides.

options.misconception: ignores the 180 tonnes still moving in 2008

options.text: The phase-out largely worked, and the remaining trade is servicing the old stock rather than new use.
Imports peaked at 4,200 tonnes, so the later figures are the important ones.
options.misconception: treats the peak year as the current level

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify over-reach and substitution risks in a border adjustment
questions.stem: Memo: the district proposes a border adjustment on imported goods. Explain two ways in which it can leak or over-reach.

answer.exemplar: It can over-reach by applying a charge calculated on estimated embedded emissions, so exporters with genuinely low-carbon production may pay a rate that reflects their own country's accounting rather than the real carbon in the goods. It can also leak in the other direction, because a charge set high enough to deter imports may push firms to import a slightly different product with a higher carbon content, or to move processing to a third country where the rules do not apply. It also does nothing for services, and for domestic producers facing foreign rivals it can raise input costs without giving them the benefit of a price on their own emissions.

questions.explanation: Estimating embedded emissions can charge a firm for carbon it did not emit, and a high charge may shift demand to dirtier substitutes or processing in third countries. Neither the charge nor the policy reaches services.
questions.hint: Think about estimated carbon and dirty substitution.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an absolute figure strengthens a declared target
questions.stem: Memo: a country's target is declared in terms of a percentage against a base year. Explain why a planner should also ask for the target to be expressed in absolute tonnes.

answer.exemplar: A percentage against a base year can be met while emissions keep rising, if the economy and population grow faster than the target requires them to fall, so the commitment would not slow the underlying pressure on climate at all. Expressing the same commitment in tonnes makes the implication explicit, forces the comparison against other sectors and countries, and stops a change in the economy being used to argue that the target is being met. The two forms should therefore be presented together, with the base year and the boundary fixed.

questions.explanation: A percentage target can be satisfied while absolute emissions rise, hiding the underlying pressure on climate. An absolute figure forces comparisons across sectors and stops economic growth being used to claim the target is met.
questions.hint: Ask what the percentage means in tonnes.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Total the revenue from a border adjustment charge
questions.stem: Memo: the district's border adjustment charges importers 45 per tonne on the embedded emissions of covered imports, which total 80,000 tonnes a year. What is the annual charge collected?
questions.explanation: The charge is 45 times 80,000, which is 3,600,000 a year. It reaches only covered imports, so it says nothing about the country's own producers, who face no carbon price.
questions.hint: Multiply the charge per tonne by the embedded tonnes.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: How a cap sets a price
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a stable allowance price under an unchanged cap
questions.stem: Memo: the district's allowance price has stayed between 18 and 22 for three years while the cap has not changed. What does that stability suggest?

options.text: The cap and demand for emissions have moved together, keeping the marginal tonne steady.
The regulator has been holding the allowance price steady against the market.
options.misconception: attributes a stable price to regulatory price fixing

options.text: The scheme has stopped working, because nothing has changed in three years.
options.misconception: reads a stable price as a stalled scheme

options.text: Firms have stopped trading, which is why the price is unchanged.
options.misconception: explains a stable price by claiming trading has stopped

questions.explanation: A steady price with an unchanged cap suggests the balance of allowances available and wanted has not shifted much, so the marginal tonne keeps its value. A regulator fixing the price would undermine the signal the scheme sends.
questions.hint: With the cap fixed, look at demand for emissions.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Plan a cost-effectiveness evaluation of two measures
questions.stem: Memo: the district wants to know which of two waste measures is more cost-effective. Describe the evaluation you would carry out.

answer.exemplar: I would define the outcome in tonnes of carbon equivalent avoided over a stated period, then cost each measure on the same basis: capital and operating cost, staff time, and the administrative cost of running the scheme. I would count only tonnes that would not have occurred anyway, so households already planning to act are not credited, and I would use a counterfactual from a comparable untreated area to net that off. Finally I would record the distribution of cost across households, because a measure that is cheaper per tonne but falls on the poorest households may not be the one the district should choose.

questions.explanation: Cost-effectiveness ranks options fairly only when outcome, costs and counterfactual are identical for each. Netting off reductions that would have happened anyway prevents being paid twice for the same tonne.
questions.hint: Fix the outcome, the cost boundary and the counterfactual.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Compare a voluntary scheme's reach with its counted savings
questions.stem: Memo: the voluntary scheme reports 900 homes joined and 6,000 tonnes of savings, while the district's housing stock is 24,000 homes and total housing emissions fell 15,000 tonnes. What does the comparison show?

options.text: The scheme explains the whole fall, because the housing sector is the only one that changed.
options.misconception: attributes the entire sector fall to one voluntary scheme

options.text: The scheme's share of the fall is small, so most homes must have taken no action.
options.misconception: assumes unaccounted tonnes mean no household acted

options.text: The scheme covered 40 per cent of the stock, so it explains most of the fall.
options.misconception: confuses a share of the fall with a share of homes

options.text: The scheme's 6,000 tonnes is 40 per cent of the fall, and it covers under 4 per cent of homes.

questions.explanation: The counted savings are 40 per cent of the 15,000 tonne fall while reaching under 4 per cent of homes, so per household the effect is comparatively large. Neither figure settles causation on its own.
questions.hint: Divide savings by the fall and homes by the stock.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A flat cap against a growing sector
questions.learningObjective: Identify the practical threat a flat cap poses to a growing sector

stimulus.body: A sector outlook for the district's ceramics industry notes that output is expected to grow 2 per cent a year to 2035, that most of the new capacity will use electric kilns, and that the sector's allowance allocation has not been adjusted since 2010. It adds that two large plants have said they would close if the allowance price exceeded 60.

questions.stem: Which feature of the outlook most threatens the cap's practical operation?

options.text: The shift to electric kilns, since electricity is more emissions-intensive than gas.
options.misconception: assumes electricity firing is dirtier than gas firing

options.text: The closure threat at an allowance price of 60, given the cap tightens as output grows.
The 2 per cent annual output growth, since any growth at all breaks a cap.
options.misconception: treats modest sector growth as an immediate threat to a cap

options.text: The fact that allowances have not been adjusted since 2010, since adjustment is legally required.
options.misconception: assumes allowance allocations must be revised on a schedule

questions.explanation: The cap tightens by default as output grows, so the allowance price can reach a level where large plants close, meaning the cap is met by shrinking activity rather than cleaning up. The kiln change and the review gap are background.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when the allowance price gets high.
